properties.name: The version guard asks the store whether a retired type is actually there, instead of refusing because the stamp names it
properties.rationale:
THE CAUSE, AND I HAD IT WRONG THE FIRST TIME. I reported that the guard could not see the data because the decision was taken before the store opened. Measured: the store is opened ONE LINE EARLIER, and `holds_a_design_probe` was already probing that same engine at that same point. The engine was available throughout. The guard was a pure stamp-to-stamp function and the caller simply never passed it anything else — so this was a cheap fix wearing the costume of an expensive one, and my wrong reading would have argued for deferring it.

THE CLASS is a declaration read as evidence about content. The stamp records the SCHEMA the writing binary had, so every graph written before a retirement names the retired type whether or not it ever held one — which is why this hit universally rather than rarely.

⭐ AND REFLOW2 HAD ALREADY DECIDED THIS, ONE SIDECAR OVER. `dec:sidecar-loss-guarded-by-store-evidence` is ACCEPTED and rules that a refusal must be conditioned on what the store actually holds, answered before opening. The principle was never carried to the version sidecar. That is the finding worth keeping: not that a check was too strict, but that an accepted principle stopped at the sibling it was written for.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED. The POPULATED case is covered only at the closure level — creating a real QualityGate node needs a pre-retirement binary, so the end-to-end refusal was not exercised. And the transport half of the report is untouched: a deliberate startup refusal still reaches the client as CONNECT_TIMEOUT, which is what sent every session that night to look at networking, and may have cost more than the guard itself.
properties.summary:
FIELD-REPORTED 2026-09-08 by dev_storyflow, against v0.55.1. A graph written by 0.50.0 holding ZERO QualityGate nodes across 3,130 was refused with "opening it could silently show you less of your design than it holds". The justification is false at zero instances: there is nothing to show less of. It cost a full working session — where-am-i, loop_status, detect-and-ask, root-cause and capture-session were all unavailable, and a production root-cause had to be written to file memory.

⚠️ AND IT WAS THE SECOND TIME. That user's store still carries `graph.pre-0.10.1-unreadable-2026-07-24` beside the one bricked today. A version guard has now locked this user out twice.

THE FIX. `unreadable_by` returned a finished message, so the caller could not act on WHY. It now returns a partition — Behind / Retired / None — and `check_and_stamp` takes a closure answering the one question a stamp cannot: of these retired node types, which does the graph actually HOLD? An UNKNOWN type still refuses on the stamp, because there the binary is genuinely behind and the stamp is the only evidence there is. A RETIRED type means the binary is AHEAD — it knows the type, so it asks the store and refuses only on a real population.

FOUR CONTROLS, each pinning something the fix could have broken: an unknown type still refuses and still says BEHIND; a populated retired type still refuses, naming what it holds; a population that CANNOT BE COUNTED still refuses, because a scan error must never read as zero; and retired EDGE types stay conservative, since an edge is not addressable by a node scan.

OBSERVED TO FAIL FIRST: the test was written against the unfixed code and reproduced the reporter's error text verbatim, including the 0.50.0/0.55.1 version pair. Then verified end to end on a forged copy of their exact situation — stamp saying 0.50.0 and naming QualityGate, store holding none — which now opens.
